zone: Sawtooth Ridge and the Lake Chelan shore
_areas_note: The Sawtooth crest is the divide between the Twisp River and Lake Chelan, and it is served from three directions rather than one. On the north, the Twisp River road reaches Scatter Creek (Abernathy), Reynolds Creek off the Mystery Campground bridge (Reynolds), War Creek, and the Eagle Creek-Oval trailhead (Oval, Courtney, Star from the north). On the south the roads are a completely different drive out of the lower Methow on Highway 153 and the Gold Creek loop, not the Twisp River at all: Libby Creek serves Hoodoo and Raven Ridge, and Crater Creek / Eagle Lakes serves Switchback, Raven Ridge and Hoodoo from the south. Anyone told to 'drive the Twisp River road' for Hoodoo, Raven Ridge or Switchback will drive to the wrong end of the range. Note also that two different trailheads carry an Eagle name and they are an hour apart: Eagle Creek-Oval on the Twisp River, and Eagle Lakes off Crater Creek in the south. On the lake side the same crest is reached by passenger ferry to the flag stops at Prince Creek and Moore Point, and from there by the Chelan Summit and Fish Creek trails - a genuine second access system for Star, Courtney, Oval and Hoodoo, with its own permit picture and its own booking constraint. MARTIN PEAK HAS BEEN REMOVED. The stored coordinate and the West Ridge route are the 8,511 ft Martin Peak immediately east of Bonanza above Holden Lake, reached by ferry to the Lucerne landing and the Holden Village bus up Railroad Creek. It shares nothing with this zone but the lake itself, and it belongs with Bonanza in the Entiat and Holden file. This is a namesake trap worth recording: a second, unrelated Martin Peak of about 8,375 ft really does sit in the Sawtooth above Cooney Lake on the Crater Creek side, so the name alone cannot tell the two apart - only the coordinate and the route can. Devore and Tupshin are kept only because the Stehekin landing was named as a zone trailhead. They are honestly a separate unit: they stand west of Lake Chelan on the ridge between Company Creek and Devore Creek, inside the National Park Service complex rather than the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness, and are approached from the Stehekin landing by shuttle and the Company Creek road. They share the ferry with the Sawtooth peaks and nothing else, and would sit better in their own Stehekin file. Mount Bigelow was added after a later pass established it goes from the Crater Creek trailhead on the Gold Creek road via the Eagle Lake trail — Upper Eagle Lake and Horsehead Pass, already in this file — rather than from the Twisp River.

sites.name: Scatter Lake basin
sites.capacity: Several established tent sites around the lake, plus a stock camp in the meadow about a mile below it. Small basin, and it fills on larch weekends in late September and early October.
sites.water: The lake itself, and Scatter Creek is beside the trail for most of the climb. This is one of the more reliable water situations in the zone.
sites.permit: No wilderness permit is needed to hike or camp on the Forest Service side of this range. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park at the Scatter Creek trailhead. Fill in the trailhead register where one is present. Firewood is scarce and the lakeshore vegetation is fragile, so treat this as a stove-only camp regardless of whether a formal fire ban is posted, and expect an actual east-side fire restriction from midsummer into September in most years.
sites.notes: This is the camp for Abernathy Peak and it sits directly under both of its routes. From Twisp the Twisp River road runs about 22 miles, turning off on an unpaved spur immediately after the Scatter Creek crossing; pavement ends several miles before that. The trail is a hard 4.6 miles with roughly 3,800 ft of gain to a lake just under 7,000 ft, so most parties either take the whole day to reach it or accept a long day out and back. From camp the South Ridge is the straightforward line, a steep loose scree slog above the lake, and the North Ridge is reached by working around the basin. The whole face above the lake has a southern aspect and is normally snow free from early July; before that, expect firm snow in the gully and an ice axe is not optional. Late September and the first week of October is the classic window here for the larch, and it is also when the basin is busiest. Bring what you need for a cold dry camp: this is east-side country, the nights are colder than the drive up suggests, and there is no shelter of any kind.

sites.name: Reynolds Creek upper basin
sites.capacity: Informal sites in the upper basin, a handful of parties at most. No numbered sites, no toilet, nothing built.
sites.water: Reynolds Creek runs through the basin and is the reason to camp here rather than higher. Filter it. Above the basin the slopes are dry talus and scree with nothing until you are back down.
sites.permit: Forest Service ground, no overnight permit needed. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the trailhead. Stove only in practice - fires are usually restricted here through the dry months and there is little to burn.
sites.notes: The obvious camp for the Reynolds Peak scramble, and it turns an 11-mile day with 5,300 ft of gain into a comfortable two. Access is easy to get wrong: drive the Twisp River road about 19 miles to Mystery Campground, cross the river there on the forest road, and follow it a little over a mile to a junction and then to the Reynolds Creek trailhead at around 3,100 ft. Mystery Campground itself is the fallback if you arrive late and want a roadside night before starting. Follow the Reynolds Creek trail on the north side of the creek to somewhere above 4,800 ft, where a log crossing puts you into the basin. Camp there, with water and views, and the summit is then a scree and talus grind to a short easy scramble through the summit rocks. Snow lingers in the upper basin later than the sunny Sawtooth crest to the south because this side faces roughly north, so early July trips should expect snow on the approach slopes. The valley has burned in places in recent seasons and blowdown on the lower trail is a recurring nuisance; check the current trail report rather than assuming a clean tread.

sites.name: Oval Lakes basin - West and Middle Oval
sites.capacity: Good sites all around West Oval, with a marked pit toilet, and stock camping with grazing in the basin above Middle Oval. The largest camping capacity in the northern half of the range.
sites.water: The lakes. Reliable all season. The long climb in from Eagle Creek has water low down and then very little, so carry enough for the ascent.
sites.permit: No overnight permit on the Forest Service side. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at the Eagle Creek-Oval trailhead. Pack out your own toilet paper even where a pit toilet exists. Fires are a bad idea here even when legal, and are usually banned outright by August.
sites.notes: This is the base for Oval Peak and the northern approach to Courtney and Star, all three of which are walk-and-scramble summits off the Chelan Summit trail once you are on the crest. It is not a casual trip: about 20 miles round trip with close to 6,700 ft of gain, up an old moraine below Gray Peak, onto the Chelan Summit trail, over a pass east of Gray Peak, and down into the basin where the maintained trail ends at Middle Oval. Much of that approach burned in the 2018 Crescent Mountain fire and is now open, dusty and hot with standing snags; do it early in the day, expect no shade, and be wary of dead trees in wind. From camp the Oval Peak scramble is short, and a fit party can link Courtney and Star along the crest, though it is a long day. Late July through early October is the practical season, with the larch turning in late September. The same basin can be reached from the lake side by ferry to Moore Point and up Fish Creek, which is the way in for a party that would rather ride a boat than drive the Twisp River road.

sites.name: Libby Lake
sites.capacity: A few small sites below the lake, and rougher ground around it. Room for two or three parties without crowding; the shoreline is fragile and there is little flat ground.
sites.water: The lake, and Libby Creek along the trail below. The last several hundred feet of the climb are dry.
sites.permit: Forest Service, no overnight permit. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Libby Lake trailhead. This is a high, sparse, slow-growing basin; carry a stove and do not build a fire, and expect a formal restriction across the lower Methow through the summer.
sites.notes: The camp for both Raven Ridge routes and the usual base for Hoodoo Peak. Getting here is a different drive from the Twisp River trailheads: from Twisp go east on Highway 20 then south on Highway 153 about nine miles and turn up the Libby Creek road. The trail is a steep 5.3 miles to a lake at roughly 7,600 ft, gaining well over 3,000 ft, and it passes the remains of an old cabin at around four miles that makes a lower alternative camp if you run out of daylight or want water lower down. Raven Ridge rises about 800 ft directly above the lake, and the standard gully-and-ridge line starts from the shore, so this is as close as a camp gets to a route in this range. Hoodoo is a scramble from the same basin, and strong parties climb both in a day from here. The upper basin holds snow into July and the gullies can be firm and unpleasant early; late August through the first half of October is the good window, and the larch here is as good as anywhere in the Sawtooth. It is exposed and treeless at the lake, so a camp below the outlet is more comfortable in wind.

sites.name: Upper Eagle Lake and Horsehead Pass
sites.capacity: Many sites - almost every level spot around Upper Eagle Lake gets used, plus a large horse camp just below it and further sites at Lower Eagle Lake about a mile off the main trail. This is the busiest backcountry camping in the range.
sites.water: Both Eagle Lakes, and Eagle Creek is bridged on the way up. Above the lakes, on the pass and along the crest, there is nothing; carry water for any traverse day.
sites.permit: Forest Service, no overnight permit needed. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Eagle Lakes / Crater Creek trailhead. This trail is open to motorcycles and stock as well as walkers, which surprises people. Fires are restricted most summers and firewood at 7,000 ft is not a renewable resource here.
sites.notes: The hub of the southern Sawtooth and the practical base for Switchback Mountain, with Hoodoo and Raven Ridge also within reach along the crest. Access is the Gold Creek side, not the Twisp River: turn off the highway onto the North Fork Gold Creek road, then a signed spur for several miles to the Eagle Lakes trailhead at about 4,760 ft. It is roughly 12.5 miles round trip to Upper Eagle Lake at 7,110 ft with only about 2,350 ft of gain, so it is a gentle carry by the standards of this range. Lower Eagle Lake at about 6,490 ft is the quieter option. Horsehead Pass at roughly 7,540 ft sits just above camp and is the gateway both to Boiling Lake on the far side and to the ridge walking that reaches Switchback. Linking on to Martin Lakes and Cooney Lake makes a longer circuit that takes in more of the southern summits. Season is roughly July into October; the pass holds snow on its north side later than the approach suggests. Be aware that Upper Eagle can be crowded and noisy on a fine weekend - if you want quiet, camp at Lower Eagle or push over the pass.

sites.name: Boiling Lake basin
sites.capacity: Established sites at the lake and near the outlet, clearly heavily used. Room for several parties. No facilities.
sites.water: The lake and its outlet, reliable through the season. The Chelan Summit trail on either side is long and dry in places, so fill here.
sites.permit: Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness, Forest Service, so no overnight permit. If you arrive by boat and stay on the trail system you need no permit at all; if you drive, a Northwest Forest Pass covers the parking. Expect fire restrictions from midsummer, and treat the basin as stove only in any case.
sites.notes: The high camp for Star Peak and Courtney Peak, sitting on the west side of the crest under Sawtooth Ridge, and the natural meeting point of the two access systems. From the road it is reached over Horsehead Pass from Upper Eagle Lake in a short day. From the water it is the first high camp on the Chelan Summit trail after the long climb up from the Prince Creek boat landing, which is where most multi-day traverses of this range put their first night on the crest. Both Star and Courtney are scrambles from here and the pair is a reasonable single day. The position is the value: it is high, it is on the crest, and it is on water, which in this dry east-side range is an unusual combination. It is popular and it shows, so camp on existing ground rather than making new. Season is roughly mid-July to mid-October. There is no shelter and no trees worth the name at the lake, so plan for wind, and for a cold clear night at this elevation even in August.

sites.name: Prince Creek Campground - boat-in
sites.capacity: A developed lakeside camp with tables, fire grates and a toilet. Sizeable, and the standard first or last night for anyone traversing the range from the water.
sites.water: Prince Creek and the lake. From here the Chelan Summit trail climbs thousands of feet with long dry stretches - this is the last easy water for a long time, so leave with full bottles.
sites.permit: Forest Service, and no permit is needed to hike or camp along this stretch if you have been dropped by boat. The rules change further up the lake: the National Park Service boundary sits between here and Stehekin, and any camp inside the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area - Flick Creek, Weaver Point and everything nearer the head of the lake - needs a North Cascades backcountry permit, which is itinerary-based, allocated partly by an early-season lottery for the peak months and partly walk-up. Fires are permitted in the established grates here, but open fires are banned outright at several of the Park Service camps up-lake, and a valley-wide ban is common by late summer. The real constraint is the ferry: the up-lake passenger boat must be booked ahead in season, Prince Creek is a request stop rather than a scheduled one and can be skipped in poor conditions, and a missed pickup on the return means a long walk to Stehekin.
sites.notes: The lake-side gateway to Star, Courtney and the southern crest. The boat drops you at roughly 1,100 ft, lake level, and the Chelan Summit trail climbs from there toward Boiling Lake and the Sawtooth crest - a serious first day in heat, on a south-facing slope, with almost no shade. Most parties land in the afternoon, camp here, and start the climb at first light. The other useful boat stop is Moore Point, about ten miles further up-lake and five and a half below Stehekin, a smaller camp with a dock, a picnic shelter, food storage and a toilet, from which the Fish Creek trail climbs to Round Lake and the Oval Lakes country - that is the water-side way to Oval Peak. The Lakeshore trail connecting the two took heavy damage in the storms of December 2025, with debris flows and washouts between Prince Creek and Moore Point, and Moore Point has also been closed at times for post-fire flood risk, so confirm both the camp and the trail are open before committing to an itinerary that depends on walking between them. The lake side is snow-free far earlier than the crest, often from April, which makes it the way in for an early-season trip.

sites.name: Bird Creek Camp, Devore Creek trail
sites.capacity: Three small tent openings and a fire ring - room for perhaps four small tents. Very small, and there is no overflow.
sites.water: Bird Creek is immediately past the camp; the site sits about a hundred feet short of the crossing. Below here, Devore Creek is the last dependable water on the climb, so fill there if you are unsure. Parties going higher can camp near 5,800 ft in the Bird Creek drainage, where there is water in early and mid-season but which can dry out late.
sites.permit: This is inside the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area, so a North Cascades backcountry permit is required year-round for the overnight, tied to a specific camp and itinerary. Peak-season demand is high enough that an early-access lottery governs the best dates and the odds are poor; plan around it rather than hoping. Open fires are banned at several camps in this unit and restricted to established pits elsewhere, and a total ban is normal by late summer. The ferry and the Stehekin shuttle are the other half of the planning: the boat must be booked, the shuttle up the valley runs a limited seasonal schedule, and the Company Creek road trailhead is several miles from the landing, so missing a bus costs you a half day on foot.
sites.notes: This is the camp for Devore Peak and Tupshin Peak, and it is worth being clear that these two are not a Sawtooth trip. They stand west of Lake Chelan on the long ridge dividing Company Creek and Hilgard Creek from Devore Creek, and everything about them - the wilderness, the permit system, the transport - is different from the Twisp River peaks. The usual way in is a ferry to the Stehekin landing, then the Company Creek road, with the Devore Creek trail reached from Weaver Point on the far side of the head of the lake; Bird Creek Camp sits about four miles up that trail at around 4,200 ft. From here Tupshin's South Ridge and Devore's Southeast Ridge are both reachable, and parties commonly climb both from the same base, either from this camp or from a higher bivouac around 5,800 ft in the Bird Creek basin. Both are steep, brushy and loose by reputation and neither is a walk-up. The season is roughly late July into early October; the approach is low, hot and overgrown early, and the upper slopes hold snow. This is the least forgiving logistics in the zone - a party that misses a boat or a bus loses a day at each end - so build slack into the itinerary and carry more food than the schedule strictly needs.
